provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Coding concepts
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to state what a sequence is in coding.
The pupils should be able to explain the purpose of loops in programming.
The pupils should be able to solve simple block coding tasks.

Introduction:
Today we will learn about coding concepts. We have used computers before but now we will learn how to give them instructions.

Content:
A sequence is a set of steps done in order. Like when you wake up, brush your teeth, then eat breakfast. Loops repeat actions. Like when you sing "Happy Birthday" twice. Block coding uses puzzle pieces to code without typing. We will use Scratch like building with blocks to make a cat move in a square.

Class activity:
In pairs, use Scratch blocks to make the sprite move in a square path.

Evaluation questions:
What is a sequence in coding?
How is a loop different from a sequence?
Make the sprite move forward 10 steps and turn right 90 degrees four times.

Summary:
Sequences are ordered steps and loops repeat actions.

topics.title: Scratch project
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to build a simple game in Scratch.
The pupils should be able to identify and fix errors in their code.

Introduction:
We have learned coding basics. Now we will use Scratch to make a game and learn to fix problems.

Content:
To build a game, we need sprites, backgrounds, and code. A sprite is a character like a cat or a ball. We add code blocks to make it move and react. When we find errors, we debug. Debugging means finding and fixing mistakes. Like when the ball goes through the wall instead of bouncing.

Class activity:
Create a simple catching game where you control a basket to catch falling fruits.

Evaluation questions:
What is a sprite in Scratch?
How do you make a sprite move when you press a key?
What might cause a sprite to disappear and how can you fix it?

Summary:
Building games in Scratch helps us learn coding by doing.

topics.title: Algorithms
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to explain what an algorithm is.
The pupils should be able to write step - by - step instructions for a simple task.

Introduction:
We have given instructions to computers. Today we learn how to write clear instructions called algorithms.

Content:
An algorithm is a set of steps to solve a problem. Like a recipe for making jollof rice. It must be clear and in order. We write algorithms for everything from brushing teeth to using an ATM. Good algorithms are efficient, meaning they don't take extra steps. Like going to the market directly instead of walking around the whole town.

Class activity:
Write an algorithm for making a cup of tea or buying plantain at the market.

Evaluation questions:
What is an algorithm?
Why must steps in an algorithm be in order?
Write an algorithm for borrowing a library book.

Summary:
Algorithms help us solve problems with clear steps.

topics.title: Databases basics
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify records and fields in a database.
The pupils should be able to create a simple class database.

Introduction:
We have used computers to store information. Today we learn how databases organize this information.

Content:
A database is an organized collection of information. It has records and fields. A record is all information about one thing, like one student's details. A field is one piece of information, like a student's name or age. Our class register is a simple database. We can make a database of all students with fields like name, age, and favorite subject.

Class activity:
Create a database of all pupils in class with fields for name, age, and favorite food.

Evaluation questions:
What is a record in a database?
What is a field in a database?
How many fields would you need in a database for school books?

Summary:
Databases help us organize information in records and fields.

topics.title: Email and cloud
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to attach files to an email and share it.
The pupils should be able to organize files in cloud storage.

Introduction:
We send messages and store files. Today we learn how to use email and the cloud to share and organize our work.

Content:
Email is electronic mail. We can attach files like pictures or documents to share. The cloud is internet storage. Google Drive is like a digital locker. We organize files in folders, like keeping yam and rice separate in the kitchen. This helps us find things easily later.

Class activity:
Create a folder in a cloud storage app and upload three different types of files into it.

Evaluation questions:
What is the cloud in computing?
How do you attach a file to an email?
Why is organizing files important?

Summary:
Email and cloud storage help us share and organize digital files.

topics.title: Internet safety
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to create strong passwords.
The pupils should be able to explain why privacy is important online.

Introduction:
The internet is useful but we must stay safe. Today we learn how to protect ourselves online.

Content:
A strong password has letters, numbers, and symbols. Like P6@2023! We should not share passwords. Privacy means keeping our personal information safe. Like not telling strangers our home address or where our parents work. We should not click suspicious links that promise free money or gifts.

Class activity:
Create a strong password for a pretend email account and explain why it's strong.

Evaluation questions:
What makes a password strong?
Why should you not share your password with friends?
What information should you keep private online?

Summary:
Good passwords and privacy habits keep us safe on the internet.

topics.title: Multimedia
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to edit photos and simple audio files.
The pupils should be able to create a short audio jingle.

Introduction:
We see and hear many things on computers. Today we learn how to edit photos and sound to make our own multimedia.

Content:
Multimedia means using different media types like text, images, and sound. We can edit photos by cropping or adding filters. Like making a photo brighter or cutting out extra parts. Audio editing means changing sound levels or cutting parts. Like making a shorter version of a song. A jingle is a short catchy tune for our class.

Class activity:
Record and edit a short jingle for our class using simple audio software.

Evaluation questions:
What is multimedia?
How can you improve a dark photo?
What makes a good jingle?

Summary:
Multimedia editing helps us create and improve digital content.

topics.title: Networking basics
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to differentiate between LAN and the internet.
The pupils should be able to explain how data travels between devices.

Introduction:
Computers often connect to each other. Today we learn how they share information through networks.

Content:
A LAN is a Local Area Network, like computers in our classroom connected. The internet is a global network connecting millions of computers. Data travels in packets, like small parcels. When you send a message, it breaks into packets, travels through different paths, and reassembles at the destination. Like sending many small danfo buses instead of one big truck.

Class activity:
Draw a diagram showing how data might travel from a computer in our class to one in another school.

Evaluation questions:
What is the difference between LAN and internet?
How does data travel between devices?
Why might sending data take time?

Summary:
Networks connect computers and share data in packets.

topics.title: AI awareness
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to list things AI can and cannot do.
The pupils should be able to use a chatbot wisely.

Introduction:
Computers can now seem intelligent. Today we learn about Artificial Intelligence and its limits.

Content:
AI means Artificial Intelligence, where computers seem smart. AI can recognize photos, answer questions, and play games. But AI cannot truly understand feelings or think creatively. Like a calculator can solve math but cannot invent new math. Chatbots are AI programs that talk to us. We should not share personal information with them and remember they don't understand like humans.

Class activity:
Use a simple chatbot to ask three questions and record the answers.

Evaluation questions:
What is AI?
Can AI feel happy or sad?
What should you not tell a chatbot?

Summary:
AI is helpful but has limits and we must use it wisely.

topics.title: Revision and project
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to demonstrate their Scratch game.
The pupils should be able to participate in an ICT exhibition.

Introduction:
We have learned many ICT skills. Today we review and share our work with others.

Content:
We will show our Scratch games to the class. An exhibition means showing our work. We explain how we made our projects and what we learned. This helps us practice speaking and sharing ideas. Like when farmers show their harvest at the market to sell and get advice.

Class activity:
Set up stations around the class where pupils can demonstrate their Scratch games to visitors.

Evaluation questions:
What was the most challenging part of making your game?
What did you learn from others' projects?
How has ICT helped you this term?

Summary:
Sharing our projects helps us learn from each other and celebrate our progress.
